head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: A summary of the subtree: whether it is a valid BST (Binary Search Tree), how many nodes it has, and its smallest and largest value
A parent needs facts about both children before it can decide
An empty tree is a BST of size 0 whose min is +infinity and max is -infinity
The sentinel values make the comparison `lmax < node.val < rmin` pass automatically for missing children
`lb and rb and lmax < node.val < rmin`
Both children are BSTs and the node sits between the left maximum and the right minimum
Checking the BST rule with only the summaries
Size of the BST rooted here, and the running answer
Tracking a global maximum from inside the recursion
Lets the inner function assign to the outer variable `best`
Updating an outer counter from a nested function
Not a BST, so the parent cannot be one either

p: `root = [10,5,15,1,8,null,7]`. Nodes are finished bottom-up (left, right, then the node).
The answer is `3`, the subtree rooted at `5`.

bullets: Time: O(n), each node is visited once and does O(1) work.
Space: O(h) for the recursion stack, where h is the height of the tree.

333.takeaway: Post-order recursion that returns (is BST, size, min, max) from each child, so a node can be checked in O(1) and the best size is tracked on the way up.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Sorted list of `[start, end]` pairs that never overlap or touch
You need a compact summary of seen numbers
Index of the first interval that starts after `value`
Finding a position in a sorted list in O(log n)
The interval just before and just after the insert position (or `None`)
Only these two neighbours can be affected
`value` already lies inside the left interval
Duplicate or already covered number: do nothing
`value` is exactly one past the left end / one before the right start
Deciding whether the new number touches a neighbour
Remove or add an interval in the list
Merging two intervals or adding a new one

p: Calls `addNum(1)`, `3`, `7`, `2`, `6`. `i` is the insert position and the table shows the list afterwards.

bullets: Time: `addNum` is O(k) here because the `starts` list is rebuilt and list insert/pop shift elements, where k is the number of intervals; `getIntervals` is O(k). A balanced tree or sorted container would make `addNum` O(log k).
Space: O(k) for the intervals.

352.takeaway: Keep a sorted list of disjoint [start, end] intervals; a binary search finds where a new number lands and it either merges with a neighbour, bridges two of them, or becomes a new interval.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Money needed to guarantee a win when the secret is somewhere in `[l, r]`
A problem on every sub-range of an array
One number or none left: guess it right away, nothing to pay
Try every number as the guess
Searching all choices of a split point
Pay `x` for a wrong guess, then the adversary sends you to the worse side
Minimax: you minimise, the secret number maximises

p: `n = 4`, the top call is `cost(1, 4)`. Sub-results used: `cost(3,4) = 3`, `cost(1,2) = 1`, `cost(1,3) = 2`, `cost(2,4) = 3`.
The minimum is `4`, so `n = 4` needs 4 dollars.

bullets: Time: O(n³), there are O(n²) ranges and each tries up to n guesses.
Space: O(n²) for the cache plus O(n) recursion depth.

375.takeaway: Interval DP: the cost of guessing in a range is the best pivot x of x + the worse of the two sides, solved with a memoised recursion.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: How many of the three character types (lowercase, uppercase, digit) are absent, found with `any(c.islower() ...)` etc.
A rule that needs at least one of each class
Splits the string into runs of equal characters (from `itertools`)
A run of length r needs `r // 3` replacements to break every triple
Breaking up long runs with the fewest edits
Too short: inserts both add length and can supply missing types, so the answer is `max(6 - n, missing)`
Length is fine: one replacement can fix a triple and a missing type at once, so `max(missing, replace)`
Must delete the excess; runs with `r % 3 == 0` need 1 deletion to save one replacement, `% 3 == 1` need 2, then others need 3
Spending forced deletions where they cancel the most replacements
All deletions plus the remaining replacements/missing types

p: Two small cases: `"aA1"` and `"aaa111"`.

bullets: Time: O(n) for the scans, since the `mod` loop does at most 3 passes over the runs.
Space: O(n) for the list of runs.

420.takeaway: Count what is missing (lower, upper, digit), what runs of three need replacing, and for long passwords spend the forced deletions on runs where they save the most replacements.

DP whose state includes a value you cannot index by (differences can be huge or negative)
Every subsequence ending at j with difference d becomes a valid length 3+ subsequence when i is appended
Counting only sequences of length at least 3
Extends all of those and adds the new pair `(j, i)` of length 2

p: `nums = [2,4,6,8,10]`. Only the pairs that add to `res` are listed (a pair adds `cnt[j][d]`).
The answer is `7`. Note that `+ 1` counts length-2 pairs but they are never added to `res` on their own.

head: i (value)
Pairs that add to res
res after i

bullets: Time: O(n²), two nested loops with O(1) dict operations.
Space: O(n²) in the worst case, since each index can store up to n different differences.

446.takeaway: `cnt[i][d]` counts arithmetic subsequences (length at least 2) that end at index i with difference d; each earlier index j extends them, and the extended ones of length 3 or more are added to the answer.

A slice with step -1 gives the reversed string

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The previous and current row of the LCS table; `cur[j+1]` is the LCS of the first `i+1` letters of `word1` and first `j+1` letters of `word2`
A DP row depends only on the row above, so keep two rows
Letters match: extend the diagonal LCS by one
No match: take the better of dropping a letter of `word1` (up) or of `word2` (left)
LCS length of the two whole strings
Reading the answer from the last cell
Everything outside the common subsequence has to be deleted from both strings
Turning LCS into a delete count

p: `word1 = "sea"`, `word2 = "eat"`. Each row is `cur` after processing a letter of `word1`; the columns are the prefixes `""`, `e`, `ea`, `eat`.
LCS is `2` ("ea"), so the answer is `3 + 3 - 2 * 2 = 2`.

bullets: Time: O(m * n) for strings of length m and n.
Space: O(n) for two rows.

583.takeaway: Minimum deletions = len(word1) + len(word2) - 2 * LCS (Longest Common Subsequence), computed with a one-row-at-a-time LCS table.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Number of permutations of the first m numbers with exactly j inversions
With one number there is one permutation with 0 inversions
Adds the entry that enters the window
Running sum over the last m entries
Removes the entry that left the window of width m
Sliding-window sum in O(1) per step
New count is the sum of `dp[j - m + 1 .. j]` modulo 10^9 + 7

p: `dp[1] = 2`: the permutations `[1,3,2]` and `[2,1,3]` have exactly one inverse pair.

bullets: Time: O(n * k), the sliding window removes the inner sum.
Space: O(k) for the two rows.

629.takeaway: DP over the number of elements: inserting the m-th number can create 0 to m-1 new inversions, so each new count is a sliding-window sum of the previous row.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: The first k+1 numbers are used for the zig-zag
You need exactly k distinct differences
Stops the second append when the pointers have crossed
The leftover numbers go in order and only add difference 1, which already appeared
Filling the rest without new distinct values

p: The loop ends because `lo > hi`. Then `5, 6` are appended, giving `[1,4,2,3,5,6]` with differences `3, 2, 1, 2, 1`, which is exactly 3 distinct values.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(n) for the output.

667.takeaway: Zig-zag between the smallest and largest unused numbers of 1..k+1 to produce k different gaps, then append the rest in increasing order (each adds a gap of 1).

Meaning

rows: 1009 independent empty lists (not copies of the same list)
Hash function: maps any key to a bucket index
Spreading keys over a fixed number of buckets; 1009 is prime, which spreads keys evenly
Add only if absent, so a set never holds duplicates
Deletes the key from its bucket if present
Linear search inside one short bucket

p: Calls `add(1)`, `add(2)`, `contains(1)`, `contains(3)`, `add(2)`, `contains(2)`, `remove(2)`, `contains(2)`.
Keys such as `1` and `1010` share bucket `1`; that is a collision, handled by the list.

Space: O(1009 + n).

705.takeaway: Separate chaining: an array of 1009 small lists, where `key % 1009` picks the list a key belongs to.

The largest value that is not `top`; `default=0` avoids an error if nothing is left

Checking a dominance condition against one number
Position of the first occurrence of the largest value
Returning an index, not a value

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The set of all sums that some k elements can make
Sizes in descending order so each element is used at most once per pass (0/1 knapsack style)
Preventing an item from being added twice
The needed sum `total * k / n` must be a whole number
Some k elements really reach that sum
One of the two groups has at most half the elements; the other group then has the same average automatically

p: The group `{1, 8}` has average 4.5, and the other six numbers sum to 27, average 4.5 as well.

bullets: Time: at most O(n² * S) where S is the total of the array, because `sums[k]` never holds more than S + 1 values.
Space: O(n * S).

805.takeaway: If a group of k elements has sum s and the same average as the whole array, then s * n = total * k; so collect every reachable sum for each group size up to n / 2 and test that one value.

Checking distinctness and range at once

Top-left corners of all 3 x 3 windows
Sliding a window over a grid

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: How much larger Bob's box must be than Alice's
Does Bob own the matching box?
First valid pair; the problem guarantees one exists

p: Derivation: after the swap, `sumA - x + y = sumB + x - y`, so `y = x + (sumB - sumA) / 2`.
`aliceSizes = [1,2,5]`, `bobSizes = [2,4]`. Sums are 8 and 6, so `delta = (6 - 8) // 2 = -1`.
Both then have 7 candies: Alice 8 - 5 + 4, Bob 6 - 4 + 5.

bullets: Time: O(n + m).
Space: O(m).

888.takeaway: If Alice gives x and gets y, equal totals force y = x + (sumBob - sumAlice) / 2, so look up that partner in a set of Bob's sizes.
